source: Lampinen, Engelcke, Li, Chaudhry, McClelland (2025) Latent learning: episodic memory complements parametric learning by enabling flexible reuse of experiences
finding: Gradient-trained models fail to use information that is only latent in their training data (reversal curse, codebooks, gridworld goals), even though they hold the pieces and can solve the task in context. A system with oracle episodic retrieval at training and test generalises to these latent tests. The paper frames this as a CLS argument: retrieval of specific episodes complements slow parametric learning.
numbers: Simple reversals and codebooks: baseline latent-test accuracy near zero while component skills (recall, in-context use) are high; only the retrieval model is above chance. Without ICL-supporting sequences in training, oracle retrieval gives only about 12% (reversals) and about 6% (codebooks). 4 runs, 95% CIs. Gridworld (RL and behaviour cloning): significant gain from retrieval but far from ceiling.
quote: the reversal curse in language modeling
limits: Oracle retrieval, small synthetic tasks, models trained from scratch; real retrieval quality not tested.
agent_relevance: Store raw episodes (old problems, old lessons) and retrieve them at test time instead of trusting only what was absorbed into weights. The model must also have practice using retrieved episodes in context.

source: Lampinen, Chaudhry, Chan, Wild, Wan, Ku, Bornschein, Pascanu, Shanahan, McClelland (2025) On the generalization of language models from in-context learning and finetuning: a controlled study
finding: On reversal, syllogism and held-out-structure datasets, putting the training set in context generalises better than finetuning on it. Finetuning can match or exceed ICL when training data is augmented with in-context inferences (local rephrase/reversal and global whole-document augmentation).
numbers: Reversal-curse dataset (Berglund): plain finetuning near zero accuracy on reversals; ICL near ceiling; augmented finetuning similarly high; ICL and augmented finetuning beat plain finetuning (t > 149, p < 1e-16). Pretrained model near chance.
quote: finetuning generalization can be improved, and in fact can even exceed ICL generalization
limits: Synthetic nonsense-word facts; ICL needs the data to fit in context; augmentation costs extra train-time compute; some regimes exist where plain finetuning generalises (reversals embedded in larger structure).
agent_relevance: Fast in-context memory plus slow weights is the LLM version of CLS. New lessons should be rehearsed together with their implications (reversals, consequences), not stored as bare facts.

source: Scialom, Chakrabarty, Muresan (2022) Fine-tuned Language Models are Continual Learners
finding: In instruction-tuned T0, mixing a tiny fraction of old data into training (rehearsal) prevents catastrophic forgetting of zero-shot ability while new tasks are learned just as well.
numbers: Rehearsal ratio r tested at 0%, 0.25%, 1% (memory buffer about 1% of 100,000 examples). At 0%: T0 zero-shot tasks catastrophically forgotten. At 0.25%: almost perfect stability. At 1%: zero-shot results stationary. New-task result unaffected by r. Also learns a sequence of new tasks (Section 4.2).
quote: with only 0.25% rehearsal we observe an almost perfect stability
limits: T0-family instruction-tuned models; needs access to a sample of the original training data.
agent_relevance: Interleaved replay works in LLMs at 0.25-1% of old data. Mixing a few old test problems into every new lesson is cheap.

source: Gupta, Therien, Ibrahim, Richter, Anthony, Belilovsky, Rish, Lesort (2024; TMLR) Simple and Scalable Strategies to Continually Pre-train Large Language Models
finding: Learning-rate re-warming, re-decaying and replay of earlier data let a continually pre-trained LLM match full re-training from scratch on final loss and benchmark averages, at a fraction of compute. Replay is the key forgetting control.
numbers: Weak shift (Pile to SlimPajama) and strong shift (English to German) at 405M parameters; weak shift confirmed at 10B. Replay used: 5% earlier data for SlimPajama, 25% for German. Cites Scialom: replay as small as 1% mitigates forgetting. Average English eval score about 47.5-48.0 with replay (figure; partly garbled in text extraction).
limits: Per-condition gaps are in figures; replay share chosen by sweep; how to select replay samples left as future work.
agent_relevance: Replay share should grow with the distance of the new data from the old.

source: Luo, Yang, Meng, Li, Zhou, Zhang (2023, v5 2025) An Empirical Study of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning
finding: Catastrophic forgetting appears in LLMs from 1B to 7B during continual instruction tuning, and it gets worse with scale in that range. Decoder-only BLOOMZ forgets less than encoder-decoder mT0. General instruction tuning before the new task reduces forgetting.
numbers: BLOOMZ 1.1b, 1.7b, 3b, 7.1b and mT0 evaluated on domain knowledge, reasoning and reading comprehension. In one table (columns not fully verified) BLOOMZ-7.1b scores 65.82 initial vs 60.61 after tuning, 7.15 difference; BLOOMZ-3b 63.90 vs 62.14.
quote: as the model scale increases, the severity of forgetting intensifies
limits: Only up to 7B; sequential fine-tuning without replay is the main condition; larger models start higher so there is more to lose.
agent_relevance: Sequential fine-tuning on new lessons with no interleaving is expected to erase old skill; test old problems after every update.

source: Rolnick, Ahuja, Schwarz, Lillicrap, Wayne (2019) Experience Replay for Continual Learning (CLEAR)
finding: CLEAR mixes on-policy learning (plasticity) with off-policy replay plus behavioural cloning on stored experience (stability) in deep RL. It nearly removes forgetting on DMLab and Atari task sequences; the behavioural cloning terms matter.
numbers: Uses a 50-50 mix of new and replayed experience; performance not very sensitive to the ratio (75-25 and 100% replay also work). Buffer 5M vs 50M behaves similarly. Ablating behavioural cloning on replay brings forgetting back (three cyclic DMLab tasks).
limits: Results table in the extraction is interleaved so per-row numbers are uncertain; RL only.
agent_relevance: A fast learner on new data plus a term that holds outputs on stored old data is the practical CLS recipe: old examples should constrain outputs, not just be seen.

source: Chaudhry, Rohrbach, Elhoseiny, Ajanthan, Dokania, Torr, Ranzato (2019) On Tiny Episodic Memories in Continual Learning
finding: Jointly training on current examples plus a tiny episodic memory (ER) beats specially designed CL methods on four benchmarks and does not overfit the memory; repeated training on the memory even improves generalisation.
numbers: Gains between 7% and 17% when the memory holds a single example per class; each training example seen once.
quote: repetitive training on even tiny memories of past tasks does not harm generalization
limits: Single-pass settings, image and small benchmarks; not language.
agent_relevance: One stored exemplar per past lesson can be enough to guard against forgetting.

source: van de Ven and Tolias (2019) Three scenarios for continual learning
finding: When the model must infer which task an input belongs to (class-incremental), regularisation methods such as EWC fail completely and only replay-based methods work. This supports the CLS claim that interleaved replay, not weight protection, prevents interference.
numbers: Split MNIST Class-IL: None 19.90%, EWC 20.01, Online EWC 19.96, SI 19.99, LwF 23.85, DGR 90.79, DGR+distill 91.79, iCaRL 94.57, Offline 97.94. Permuted MNIST Class-IL: None 17.26, EWC 25.04, Online EWC 33.88, DGR 92.19, DGR+distill 96.38, offline 97.59. 20 seeds.
limits: MNIST scale; generative replay quality may degrade on harder data (not tested here).
agent_relevance: When the agent cannot be told which old lesson a new problem belongs to, only rehearsal of old problems protects it.

source: Kemker and Kanan (2018) FearNet: Brain-Inspired Model for Incremental Learning
finding: A dual-memory network (hippocampus-like fast store, mPFC-like slow network, amygdala-like gate) with sleep-phase generative replay beats iCaRL and others on incremental class learning without storing raw examples.
numbers: Normalised to offline MLP, all-class: CIFAR-100 0.947 (iCaRL 0.749), CUB-200 0.891 (iCaRL 0.864), AudioSet 0.932 (iCaRL 0.733); mean 0.923 vs iCaRL 0.782. Offline MLP accuracy 69.9%, 59.8%, 45.8%. With an oracle gate: 1.002, 0.936, 0.972. Sleeps every 10 study sessions by default; fewer sleeps hurt.
limits: Gate errors cost about 5 points on CIFAR-100; struggles when base knowledge is weak (AudioSet as base then CIFAR: all-class 0.634); pretrained features.
agent_relevance: Consolidation timing is a knob (batch it), and a router that decides between fresh memory and consolidated knowledge is a failure point.

source: Arani, Sarfraz, Zonooz (2022; ICLR) Learning Fast, Learning Slow: A General Continual Learning Method based on Complementary Learning System (CLS-ER)
finding: CLS-ER keeps two EMA models over a working model (plastic: fast EMA, stable: slow EMA) plus an episodic buffer; the semantic memories supply logits for replayed samples. It beats DER++ and other rehearsal methods; the stable model is best at old tasks.
numbers: S-Tiny-ImageNet buffer 200, Class-IL: +176% relative to ER and +114% relative to DER++. Appendix, stable vs working vs plastic: R-MNIST 66.19 vs 50.09 vs 62.68; P-MNIST 75.22 vs 63.09 vs 71.32; GCIL-CIFAR-100 uniform 23.47 vs 9.97 vs 17.19.
limits: Largest gains in tightest memory settings; vision only; hyperparameters tuned per buffer size.
agent_relevance: A slowly averaged stable copy of knowledge beats a fast-updated one on old tasks; keep a slow record for long-term and a fast one for recent.

source: Pham, Liu, Hoi (2021) DualNet: Continual Learning, Fast and Slow
finding: CLS-inspired split: a slow self-supervised learner for task-agnostic representation and a fast supervised learner adapting it; reported to beat ER, DER++ and CTN on CORE50 and miniImageNet by a large margin.
numbers: Split miniImageNet, task-aware: ER ACC 53.43 (forgetting 11.21); DER++ 62.32; CTN 65.82; with augmentation ER 59.80, DER++ 63.48, CTN 68.04. 5 runs. DualNet rows not captured in extracted text.
limits: DualNet figures not extracted; one-epoch online setting.
agent_relevance: Separate slow general skill from fast task-specific adaptation; only the second changes per lesson.

source: Buzzega, Boschini, Porrello, Abati, Calderara (2020) Dark Experience Replay for General Continual Learning
finding: Replaying stored logits (distilling the past network) is a strong, simple baseline that beats ER, MER, A-GEM-R and GSS; it is the baseline CLS-ER and others compare to.
numbers: MNIST-360 buffer 200: ER 49.27, MER 48.58, A-GEM-R 28.34, GSS 43.92, DER 55.22, DER++ 54.16; buffer 500: ER 65.04, DER 69.11, DER++ 69.62 (column mapping inferred from extracted text); SGD 19.09, JOINT 82.98.
limits: Table reflows in extraction; vision benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Store the old model's outputs, not only inputs and labels; replaying outputs transfers behaviour.

source: Gutierrez, Shu, Gu, Yasunaga, Su (2024; NeurIPS) HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for Large Language Models
finding: Maps hippocampal indexing theory to a RAG pipeline: LLM as neocortex extracting triples, a knowledge graph with Personalized PageRank as hippocampal index (pattern separation and completion). Improves multi-hop retrieval and QA over dense retrieval and complements IRCoT.
numbers: Single-step retrieval: +11 and +20 points R@2 and R@5 on 2WikiMultiHopQA, about +3 on MuSiQue; HotpotQA competitive but lower. QA F1 gains up to 3, 17, 1 points on MuSiQue, 2Wiki, HotpotQA. Up to 20% over SOTA retrieval; 10-30x cheaper and 6-13x faster than IRCoT online.
limits: Non-parametric: weights never change, so it is not consolidation. Weaker on HotpotQA (low integration need). Depends on OpenIE quality.
agent_relevance: An external fast store with graph links gives cross-item integration cheaply; fits a retrieval step that tests new lessons against old problems.

source: Gutierrez, Shu, Gu, Yasunaga, Su (2025; ICML) From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for Large Language Models (HippoRAG 2)
finding: Structure-augmented RAG methods fall below plain dense retrieval on simple factual memory; HippoRAG 2 adds passage nodes, recognition-memory filtering and query-to-triple matching and beats a strong dense baseline on factual, sense-making and associative tasks.
numbers: 7% improvement on associative memory over the best baseline (NV-Embed-v2); +9.5% F1 on 2Wiki and +3.1% on LV-Eval vs NV-Embed-v2; Recall@5 +12.5% over NER-to-node linking. Factual memory not degraded.
limits: Non-parametric only; no weight-forgetting test; relies on a strong embedder and LLM triple extraction.
agent_relevance: Added structure must not hurt plain similarity recall; check that basic factual lookup does not degrade.

source: Das, Chaudhury et al. (2024; ICML) Larimar: Large Language Models with Episodic Memory Control
finding: A distributed episodic memory (motivated by CLS) attached to a frozen LLM allows one-shot knowledge edits, sequential editing, selective forgetting and input-length generalisation without finetuning.
numbers: Edits 4-10x faster than ROME and GRACE (abstract: 8-10x depending on base LLM). Rewrite accuracy near 100% up to 512 edits (memory size K), drops to 82% at 1024. Writing two rephrases lifts generalisation from 70.4% to 82.2%. Surpasses GRACE in generalisation at about 600 edits.
limits: Memory capacity is a hard limit; narrow editing benchmarks (CounterFact, ZsRE).
agent_relevance: A fast writable memory next to frozen weights handles single new facts; capacity limits mean pruning or consolidation is needed.

source: Park, O'Brien, Cai, Morris, Liang, Bernstein (2023) Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
finding: LLM agents with a memory stream, retrieval and periodic reflection (synthesising memories into higher-level insights, a consolidation-like step) are rated more believable than ablated versions.
numbers: 100 human raters ranked 5 conditions by believability. Condition without memory, planning or reflection: TrueSkill mu 21.21. Full architecture vs prior-work condition: effect size d = 8.16. Kruskal-Wallis H(4) = 150.29, p < 0.001. Reflections are triggered when summed importance of recent events passes a threshold, about two to three times a day.
limits: Human-rated believability, not task accuracy; two-day simulation; memory hallucination.
agent_relevance: Reflection triggered by accumulated importance (not a fixed clock) is an LLM-agent analogue of consolidation.

source: Shinn, Cassano, Berman, Gopinath, Narasimhan, Yao (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Agents write verbal reflections on failed trials into an episodic memory buffer and reuse them in the next trial: a fast, weight-free learner.
numbers: ReAct+Reflexion completes 130 of 134 AlfWorld tasks; +22% AlfWorld, +20% HotPotQA, +11% HumanEval over baselines; 91% pass@1 on HumanEval vs 80% for GPT-4.
limits: Needs a reliable success signal; lessons are reused for the same task, not tested for harm to other tasks.
agent_relevance: Verbal lessons from failures help, but nothing tests whether a lesson breaks old problems; add that check.

source: Packer, Wooders, Lin, Fang, Patil, Stoica, Gonzalez (2023) MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
finding: Tiered memory for LLM agents (main context, recall storage, archival storage) managed by the LLM through function calls, with recursive summarisation on context pressure.
numbers: Queue eviction at 70% of the context window, summary of about 50% of messages. Nested key-value retrieval: only MemGPT completes tasks beyond 2 nesting levels; MemGPT with GPT-4 Turbo does worse than with GPT-4. Exact accuracies only in figures.
limits: Needs strong function-calling models; numbers only in figures.
agent_relevance: Hot and cold memory mirrors fast and slow stores; summarisation is lossy consolidation and should be tested for what it loses.

source: Lin, Snell, Wang, Packer, Wooders, Stoica, Gonzalez (2025) Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time
finding: Offline sleep-time computation over stored context (pre-computing inferences before the query arrives) cuts test-time compute and raises accuracy. An explicit idle-time replay-like step inside an LLM agent loop.
numbers: About 5x less test-time compute for equal accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME; more sleep-time compute adds up to +13% (GSM-Symbolic) and +18% (AIME); 2.5x lower per-query cost on Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic. Gain correlates with query predictability.
limits: Needs predictable queries; synthetic stateful tasks; SWE case study is qualitative.
agent_relevance: Idle compute spent re-examining stored material pays off when future questions are guessable.

source: Kirkpatrick et al. (2017) Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks (EWC)
finding: EWC slows learning on weights important to old tasks (a synaptic-consolidation analogue) and lets a network learn permuted MNIST and a sequence of Atari games.
numbers: Ten Atari games sequentially, scored as total human-normalised score (maximum 10); EWC retains more than plain SGD (values not extracted).
limits: Fails in class-incremental settings (EWC 20.01% on split MNIST Class-IL, van de Ven and Tolias 2019). Only the setup text was read.
agent_relevance: Weight protection does not apply to a prompt-based agent; replay-style tests do.

source: Synthesis from Scialom 2022, van de Ven and Tolias 2019, Gupta 2024
finding: Dose-response of replay is steep at the low end: 0.25-1% old data restores near full stability in instruction-tuned LLMs, while regularisation-only methods stay at the no-protection floor in class-incremental settings.
numbers: Scialom: 0% forgets, 0.25% near-perfect. van de Ven: EWC 20.01 vs DGR 90.79 on split MNIST Class-IL. Gupta: 5% replay (weak shift), 25% (German).
limits: Different models and tasks; not a single controlled experiment.
agent_relevance: Keep a standing small share of old problems in every test cycle, not an occasional audit.

source: Synthesis from Luo 2023 and Gupta 2024
finding: Evidence on whether scale protects against forgetting is mixed: Luo finds forgetting rises with scale from 1B to 7B in continual instruction tuning, while Gupta finds simple replay recipes still match retraining at 10B.
numbers: Luo 1.1b to 7.1b: forgetting intensifies. Gupta: 405M and 10B both match retraining with replay plus LR re-warming.
limits: Different protocols (instruction tuning vs pre-training), so not a direct conflict.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a larger model protects itself; run old-problem checks regardless of scale.

source: Synthesis from the two Lampinen papers
finding: Both Lampinen papers share a limit: in-context or retrieval routes help only if the model has seen training examples that teach it to use context across episodes.
numbers: Latent learning paper: without ICL-supporting sequences, oracle retrieval gives about 12% (reversals) and about 6% (codebooks).
limits: Synthetic; transfer to frontier pre-trained LLMs, which already have strong ICL, is not shown.
agent_relevance: For a frontier LLM, in-context use of retrieved lessons is already trained in, so retrieving past lessons should work without extra training (untested here).
